L855: sys.modulescite251†¶ L856: This is a dictionary that maps module names to modules which have already been loaded. This can be manipulated to force reloading of modules and other tricks. However, replacing the dictionary will not necessarily work as expected and deleting essential items from the dictionary may cause Python to fail.
L857: If you want to iterate over this global dictionary always use `sys.modules.copy()` or `tuple(sys.modules)` to avoid exceptions as its size may change during iteration as a side effect of code or activity in other threads.
L858: sys.orig_argvcite16†¶ L859: 
L860: 
L861: The list of the original command line arguments passed to the Python executable.
L862: 
L863: The elements of `sys.orig_argv` are the arguments to the Python interpreter, while the elements of cite13†`sys.argv` are the arguments to the user’s program. Arguments consumed by the interpreter itself will be present in `sys.orig_argv` and missing from `sys.argv`.
L864: 
L865: Added in version 3.10.
L866: 
L867: sys.pathcite252†¶ L868: A list of strings that specifies the search path for modules. Initialized from the environment variable cite253†`PYTHONPATH` , plus an installation-dependent default.
L869: 
L870: By default, as initialized upon program startup, a potentially unsafe path is prepended to `sys.path` (before the entries inserted as a result of cite253†`PYTHONPATH` ):
L871: 
L872:   * `python -m module` command line: prepend the current working directory.
L873:   * `python script.py` command line: prepend the script’s directory. If it’s a symbolic link, resolve symbolic links.
L874: 
L875:   * `python -c code` and `python` (REPL) command lines: prepend an empty string, which means the current working directory.
L876: 
L877: To not prepend this potentially unsafe path, use the cite110†`-P` command line option or the cite254†`PYTHONSAFEPATH` environment variable.
L878: A program is free to modify this list for its own purposes. Only strings should be added to `sys.path`; all other data types are ignored during import.
L879: 
L880: See also
L881: 
L882:   * Module cite75†`site` This describes how to use .pth files to extend `sys.path`.

The initialization of the sys.path module search path — Python 3.14.7 documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys_path_init.html)
citeturn10640view3 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys_path_init.html","lineno":11}); Total lines: 57
L1: # The initialization of the cite0†`sys.path` module search pathcite1†¶ L2: 
L3: A module search path is initialized when Python starts. This module search path may be accessed at cite0†`sys.path` .
L4: 
L5: The first entry in the module search path is the directory that contains the input script, if there is one. Otherwise, the first entry is the current directory, which is the case when executing the interactive shell, a cite2†`-c` command, or cite3†`-m` module.
L6: The cite4†`PYTHONPATH` environment variable is often used to add directories to the search path. If this environment variable is found then the contents are added to the module search path.
L7: 
L8: Note
L9: 
L10: cite4†`PYTHONPATH` will affect all installed Python versions/environments. Be wary of setting this in your shell profile or global environment variables. The cite5†`site` module offers more nuanced techniques as mentioned below.
L11: The next items added are the directories containing standard Python modules as well as any cite6†extension module s that these modules depend on. Extension modules are `.pyd` files on Windows and `.so` files on other platforms. The directory with the platform-independent Python modules is called `prefix`. The directory with the extension modules is called `exec_prefix`.
L12: The cite7†`PYTHONHOME` environment variable may be used to set the `prefix` and `exec_prefix` locations. Otherwise these directories are found by using the Python executable as a starting point and then looking for various ‘landmark’ files and directories. Note that any symbolic links are followed so the real Python executable location is used as the search starting point. The Python executable location is called `home`.
L13: Once `home` is determined, the `prefix` directory is found by first looking for `python majorversion minorversion.zip` (`python311.zip`). On Windows the zip archive is searched for in `home` and on Unix the archive is expected to be in `lib`. Note that the expected zip archive location is added to the module search path even if the archive does not exist. If no archive was found, Python on Windows will continue the search for `prefix` by looking for `Lib\os.py`.
L14: Python on Unix will look for `lib/python majorversion.minorversion/os.py` (`lib/python3.11/os.py`). On Windows `prefix` and `exec_prefix` are the same, however on other platforms `lib/python majorversion.minorversion/lib-dynload` (`lib/python3.11/lib-dynload`) is searched for and used as an anchor for `exec_prefix`. On some platforms `lib` may be `lib64` or another value, see cite8†`sys.platlibdir` and cite9†`PYTHONPLATLIBDIR` .
L15: Once found, `prefix` and `exec_prefix` are available at cite10†`sys.base_prefix` and cite11†`sys.base_exec_prefix` respectively.
L16: 
L17: If cite7†`PYTHONHOME` is not set, and a `pyvenv.cfg` file is found alongside the main executable, or in its parent directory, cite12†`sys.prefix` and cite13†`sys.exec_prefix` get set to the directory containing `pyvenv.cfg`, otherwise they are set to the same value as cite10†`sys.base_prefix` and cite11†`sys.base_exec_prefix` , respectively. This is used by cite14†Virtual Environments .

citeturn10640view4 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://docs.python.org/3/reference/import.html#cached-bytecode-invalidation","lineno":190}); Total lines: 328
L185: A package’s `__init__.py` file may set or alter the package’s cite57†`__path__` attribute, and this was typically the way namespace packages were implemented prior to cite11†PEP 420†peps.python.org . With the adoption of cite11†PEP 420†peps.python.org , namespace packages no longer need to supply `__init__.py` files containing only `__path__` manipulation code; the import machinery automatically sets `__path__` correctly for the namespace package.
L186: ### 5.4.5. Module reprscite59†¶ L187: 
L188: By default, all modules have a usable repr, however depending on the attributes set above, and in the module’s spec, you can more explicitly control the repr of module objects.
L189: If the module has a spec (`__spec__`), the import machinery will try to generate a repr from it. If that fails or there is no spec, the import system will craft a default repr using whatever information is available on the module. It will try to use the `module.__name__`, `module.__file__`, and `module.__loader__` as input into the repr, with defaults for whatever information is missing.
L190: 
L191: Here are the exact rules used:
L192:   * If the module has a `__spec__` attribute, the information in the spec is used to generate the repr. The “name”, “loader”, “origin”, and “has_location” attributes are consulted.
L193: 
L194:   * If the module has a `__file__` attribute, this is used as part of the module’s repr.
L195: 
L196:   * If the module has no `__file__` but does have a `__loader__` that is not `None`, then the loader’s repr is used as part of the module’s repr.
L197: 
L198:   * Otherwise, just use the module’s `__name__` in the repr.
L199: Changed in version 3.12: Use of `module_repr()`, having been deprecated since Python 3.4, was removed in Python 3.12 and is no longer called during the resolution of a module’s repr.
L200: ### 5.4.6. Cached bytecode invalidationcite60†¶ L201: 
L202: Before Python loads cached bytecode from a `.pyc` file, it checks whether the cache is up-to-date with the source `.py` file. By default, Python does this by storing the source’s last-modified timestamp and size in the cache file when writing it. At runtime, the import system then validates the cache file by checking the stored metadata in the cache file against the source’s metadata.
L203: Python also supports “hash-based” cache files, which store a hash of the source file’s contents rather than its metadata. There are two variants of hash-based `.pyc` files: checked and unchecked. For checked hash-based `.pyc` files, Python validates the cache file by hashing the source file and comparing the resulting hash with the hash in the cache file. If a checked hash-based cache file is found to be invalid, Python regenerates it and writes a new checked hash-based cache file.
L204: For unchecked hash-based `.pyc` files, Python simply assumes the cache file is valid if it exists. Hash-based `.pyc` files validation behavior may be overridden with the cite61†`--check-hash-based-pycs` flag.

L238: The /proc/PID/maps file contains the currently mapped memory regions and their access permissions.
L239: The format is:
L240: 
L241:     address           perms offset  dev   inode      pathname
L242: 
L243:     08048000-08049000 r-xp 00000000 03:00 8312       /opt/test
L244:     08049000-0804a000 rw-p 00001000 03:00 8312       /opt/test
L245:     0804a000-0806b000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0          [heap]
L246:     a7cb1000-a7cb2000 ---p 00000000 00:00 0
L247:     a7cb2000-a7eb2000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0
L248:     a7eb2000-a7eb3000 ---p 00000000 00:00 0
L249:     a7eb3000-a7ed5000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0
L250:     a7ed5000-a8008000 r-xp 00000000 03:00 4222       /lib/libc.so.6
L251:     a8008000-a800a000 r--p 00133000 03:00 4222       /lib/libc.so.6
L252:     a800a000-a800b000 rw-p 00135000 03:00 4222       /lib/libc.so.6
L253:     a800b000-a800e000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0
L254:     a800e000-a8022000 r-xp 00000000 03:00 14462      /lib/libpthread.so.0
L255:     a8022000-a8023000 r--p 00013000 03:00 14462      /lib/libpthread.so.0
L256:     a8023000-a8024000 rw-p 00014000 03:00 14462      /lib/libpthread.so.0
L257:     a8024000-a8027000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0
L258:     a8027000-a8043000 r-xp 00000000 03:00 8317       /lib/ld-linux.so.2
L259:     a8043000-a8044000 r--p 0001b000 03:00 8317       /lib/ld-linux.so.2
L260:     a8044000-a8045000 rw-p 0001c000 03:00 8317       /lib/ld-linux.so.2
L261:     aff35000-aff4a000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0          [stack]
L262:     ffffe000-fffff000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0          [vdso]
L263: where “address” is the address space in the process that it occupies, “perms” is a set of permissions:
L264: 
L265:     r = read

L268:     s = shared

The “pathname” shows the name associated file for this mapping. If the mapping is not associated with a file:
